terms.gloss: a conservative: one who favours keeping things as they are
terms.grammar: noun phrase: fautor, fautōris m.; for a woman, fautrīx
terms.comment: A modern description in classical words, built on cōnservāre, to keep, preserve. Traupman gives optimātēs for the conservatives of ancient Rome (p. 178), but the optimātēs were the men who worked through the senate and the leading families, and the populārēs those who worked through the people’s assemblies (Cic. Sest. 96, Lewis & Short s.v. optimās): methods and alliances, not programmes. Neither is a modern conservative or liberal party, and the words are best not used for them.
Of a conservative in outlook rather than in party.

terms.gloss: conservative; as a noun, a conservative
terms.comment: Traupman’s coinage, adjective and noun; no ancient word has this form.

sources: Lewis & Short: conservo · Lewis & Short: fautor · Lewis & Short: optimas · Lewis & Short: popularis
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. conservative.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 178, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
